topic: The Physics of Pi: Colliding Blocks and Digit Emergence
target_audience: Undergraduate physics students or math enthusiasts

outline.topic: The Physics of Pi: Colliding Blocks and Digit Emergence
outline.target_audience: Undergraduate physics students or math enthusiasts

sections.title: The Hook: An Unexpected Connection
sections.content: Introduce the counter-intuitive phenomenon: two blocks of mass m and M=100^n * m colliding elastically on a frictionless surface produce exactly the first n+1 digits of pi in the total number of collisions.
sections.example: Visualize two blocks, a small one (mass 1) and a giant one (mass 100), colliding. The small block bounces off the wall and hits the large block; the total count of collisions is exactly 31.

sections.title: Prerequisite Physics: Conservation Laws
sections.content: Briefly review Elastic Collisions. Establish that in an isolated system, both Kinetic Energy (1/2mv^2) and Momentum (mv) must be conserved.
sections.example: Use a billiard ball animation: show the vector arrows for momentum before and after impact, highlighting how energy transfers perfectly between equal masses.

sections.title: The Phase Space Mapping
sections.content: Transition to the 'Phase Space' approach. Instead of tracking time, map the velocities of the two blocks as coordinates (v1, v2) on a 2D plane. The energy conservation law defines a circle (an ellipse if masses differ).
sections.example: An animated circle on a grid. As the blocks collide, the 'state' point jumps along an arc of this circle until it hits a boundary (the wall or the other block).

sections.title: Geometric Unfolding
sections.content: Explain that the collisions act like reflections inside a wedge. As the mass ratio increases, the wedge angle sharpens. The number of collisions corresponds to how many times a straight line bounces inside this angular wedge.
sections.example: Show a geometric 'wedge' diagram where the angle is theta = arctan(sqrt(m/M)). As M grows, theta approaches zero, causing the 'bouncing path' to approximate a circular arc.

sections.title: Conclusion: Why Pi?
sections.content: Connect the geometry to the result. Since the total angle of the wedge is related to pi, counting the reflections of the trajectory is mathematically equivalent to calculating the digits of pi.
sections.example: A final animation showing the collision count for M=1, 100, 10,000, and 1,000,000, revealing the digits 3, 31, 314, and 3141, respectively.

storyboard.title: The Hook: An Unexpected Connection
lecture_lines: Two blocks collide: small mass m, large mass M.
They bounce between a wall and each other.
For M=100m, we see exactly 31 collisions.
Surprisingly, this counts the digits of pi.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite Physics: Conservation Laws
lecture_lines: Elastic collisions conserve both momentum and energy.
Energy is half mass times velocity squared.
animations: Fade in label '#F8F9FA' for 'Conservation of Energy'.
Visualize energy flow as a '#20C997' smooth curve.
Highlight conserved quantity value '#FD7E14' within the curve.

storyboard.title: The Phase Space Mapping
lecture_lines: Instead of time, map velocities (v1, v2).
Collisions jump the state along this path.
animations: Fade in grid lines '#495057' representing phase space.
Map system state as a '#0D6EFD' moving point.

storyboard.title: Geometric Unfolding
lecture_lines: Collisions map to reflections in a wedge.
The wedge angle depends on mass ratio.

storyboard.title: Conclusion: Why Pi?
lecture_lines: Geometry maps reflection count to pi digits.
Higher mass ratios reveal more digits.
It's an elegant, hidden geometric law.
